# War, Occupation, and the Power of Paperwork {#sec-2-05}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act II — Land, Monopoly, and Institution · 1846–1848
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does conquest become capital?

**The answer.** Through a treaty, not a battle. The Bear Flag Revolt and the
fighting in California were minor; the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed 2
February 1848, is what mattered, because it converted military occupation into
legal ownership. California became investable not when it was conquered but when
it was documented.

**The mechanism.** Public authority converted into private property rights — the
legal substrate that every subsequent fortune in this book is built on. The $15
million paid to Mexico purchased an enforceable framework for title, which is
worth more than the land it covers.

**The key fact.** The treaty was signed on 2 February 1848. Gold had already
been found at Sutter's Mill on 24 January. The United States acquired California
nine days after it became the most valuable territory on the continent, and did
not know it.

**The human anchor.** A land commission hearing, in which a rancho family with a
Mexican grant and a hand-drawn boundary must prove title to an American court in
English.

**Excluded voices.** Californio grant-holders, who were promised the protection
of their property under the treaty and then spent decades and their fortunes
litigating for it. Indigenous Californians, for whom neither sovereign
recognised title at all. And the fact that the treaty's protective article was
altered before ratification.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that legal documentation rather than military
victory is what converts conquest into capital by showing that California's
economic transformation dates from the treaty and the land commission, not from
the fighting.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Gold was found at Sutter's Mill on 24 January 1848. The Treaty of Guadalupe
Hidalgo was signed on 2 February. For nine days the United States negotiated for
California without knowing it had become the most valuable territory on the
continent, and Mexico ceded it on the same terms.

The chapter's argument is that the treaty mattered and the fighting did not. The
Bear Flag Revolt and the California campaign were small, confused, and largely
decided elsewhere. What converted military occupation into something investable
was a legal instrument: a document establishing that title could be held,
transferred, and enforced under American law. California became capital not
because it was conquered but because it was documented, and the fifteen million
dollars paid to Mexico purchased a framework rather than a landscape.

The hinge is Article X. The treaty as negotiated contained a provision
protecting existing Mexican land grants, and it was struck before ratification.
What replaced it was a promise of protection without a mechanism, and the
mechanism turned out to be the Land Act of 1851 and a commission before which
grant-holders had to prove their title — in English, in an American court,
against a boundary drawn as a creek and an oak tree.

The result was a transfer of land accomplished procedurally rather than by
seizure. Californio families spent years and, frequently, the land itself paying
lawyers to establish ownership of property they already occupied. Some won and
were ruined by the cost of winning. That is a more durable method than
confiscation, and a much harder one to protest.

Indigenous title was recognised by neither sovereign, before or after.

The chapter's structural point closes Act II's first movement: capital requires
enforceable title, the United States supplied it, and that was the actual
acquisition. The legal framework is now in place, and the gold is already in the
river.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Beats

1. **Hook.** Nine days. The gold is found on 24 January; the treaty is signed on
   2 February. Nobody in Mexico City or Washington knows.
2. **The war, briefly.** The Bear Flag Revolt and the California campaign, kept
   short and unromantic. It is not the mechanism.
3. **Guadalupe Hidalgo.** What the treaty said, what it paid, and what it
   promised about existing property.
4. **The alteration.** Article X, struck before ratification, and what its
   removal did to Mexican land titles. This is the chapter's hinge.
5. **The Land Act of 1851 and the commission.** The burden of proof placed on
   grant-holders. Years, lawyers, and fees.
6. **How title moved.** Californio families losing land to legal costs rather
   than to seizure. The mechanism is procedural, which is why it is durable.
7. **Indigenous title.** Recognised by neither sovereign. Say so directly.
8. **Why documentation is the asset.** The chapter's argument: capital requires
   enforceable title, and the United States supplied it. That is the real
   acquisition.
9. **Landing.** The legal framework is in place. The gold is already in the
   river. Hand off.

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does conquest become capital?
:::

The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed on 2 February 1848, transferring
California to the United States for fifteen million dollars.

Gold had been found at Sutter's Mill nine days earlier.

Nobody in Mexico City knew. Nobody in Washington knew. Word reached the eastern
United States months later and was not widely believed until December, when the
president confirmed it in a message to Congress and the rush began in earnest.
For those nine days, and for a good while afterwards, the most valuable
territory on the continent changed hands at a price set in complete ignorance of
what it contained.

The coincidence is the best-known fact in California history and it is usually
told as irony. It is more useful as an argument about what the treaty actually
accomplished, because the gold was in the ground either way. What changed on 2
February was not the value of California. It was the legal system that would
determine who owned it.

## The war, briefly

The fighting in California was small and confused, and this chapter treats it as
such.

American settlers around Sonoma declared a republic in June 1846 and raised a
flag with a bear on it, an episode that lasted under a month and was overtaken
by the arrival of United States naval forces. There was resistance in the south,
notably at San Pasqual, where Californio lancers handled American dragoons
roughly. The territory was secured by January 1847 under a capitulation
negotiated at Cahuenga.

The war was decided in Mexico, not in California. What California contributed
was the reason for it: the harbour at San Francisco had been an explicit
American objective for years, and the administration in Washington had attempted
to buy it before deciding to take it.

## What the treaty did

The instrument that mattered ran to a few thousand words and did three things.

It transferred sovereignty over an enormous territory — California, Nevada,
Utah, and parts of several other future states — in exchange for fifteen million
dollars and the assumption of certain claims. It established the boundary. And
it addressed the property and citizenship of the Mexican nationals who lived
there.

That third element is the one this chapter turns on, because it is where a
military occupation becomes a system of ownership. Conquest by itself produces
control. It does not produce title, and without title there is nothing to buy,
sell, mortgage, or develop. Capital cannot operate in a territory where
ownership is a matter of who is standing on the land.

The fifteen million dollars purchased a legal framework. That is the actual
acquisition, and it is the reason California became investable in 1848 rather
than merely occupied.

## Article X

The treaty as negotiated contained an article protecting Mexican land grants in
the ceded territories. The United States Senate struck it before ratification.

What replaced it was a diplomatic statement of assurance — the Protocol of
Querétaro — indicating that grant-holders retained their rights and could assert
them in American courts. The distinction between a treaty article and an
assurance about access to litigation looks technical. It was the whole game.

Because in 1851 Congress passed the California Land Act, which established a
commission before which every holder of a Spanish or Mexican grant had to appear
and prove title. The burden of proof was on the claimant. The proceedings were
conducted in English under American rules of evidence. Decisions could be
appealed to the federal district court and then to the Supreme Court, and they
routinely were, by whichever party lost.

Consider what a Californio family had to produce. A grant document from a
government that no longer existed. A *diseño* sketching boundaries by reference
to an oak tree and a creek. Evidence of continuous occupation. Witnesses. And a
lawyer, for a process that took, on average, many years — in a number of cases
more than a decade.

## The mechanism

The outcome was a transfer of land accomplished procedurally.

Most claims were eventually confirmed. This is important and is regularly left
out: the commission was not a rubber stamp for dispossession, and the majority
of the acreage claimed was upheld. But confirmation took years, and years of
litigation had to be paid for, and the way a cattle-rich, cash-poor rancho
family paid for it was by selling or mortgaging the land at whatever price was
available during the period of uncertainty. Attorneys were frequently paid in
acreage. Squatters occupied the disputed land while the case ran, and by the
time title was confirmed there were people living on it who had improvements, a
claim in equity, and votes in a state legislature increasingly hostile to large
grants.

Families that won were ruined by winning. That is a more durable method of
transfer than confiscation and a much harder one to protest, because at every
stage it is a legal process with an appeal available.

The land ended up with American purchasers, lawyers, banks, and squatters.
Within a generation, Californio landholding in the north had largely collapsed.

## What fifteen million dollars bought

The sum deserves a moment, because it is the price at which the largest transfer
of territory in North American history was settled.

Fifteen million dollars, plus the assumption of some three and a quarter million
in claims by American citizens against Mexico, for a cession of roughly half a
million square miles. It was not a trivial amount of money in 1848 — it was
comparable to the Louisiana Purchase four decades earlier, and rather more than
the federal government's ordinary annual revenue at the time.

It was also, within eighteen months, less than the value of the gold coming out
of a single year's production in the territory it had purchased.

The chapter's argument is that this arithmetic is not the point, and that
treating it as an extraordinary bargain misunderstands the transaction. What the
United States bought was not a quantity of gold it did not know about. It was
jurisdiction: the authority to determine, through its own courts and its own
statutes, who owned what. Everything extracted from California over the
following century — the gold, the land, the timber, the water rights, the
railroad grants — was allocated under a legal system that the treaty installed.

Jurisdiction is the most valuable thing a state can acquire, and it is almost
never priced correctly, because its value depends entirely on what is done with
it afterwards.

## Citizenship

The treaty also addressed the people. Mexican nationals in the ceded territory
could retain Mexican citizenship by declaring so within a year, or become United
States citizens by default. Most became Americans, and Californios participated
in the constitutional convention the following year and in the early state
legislature; several were substantial political figures.

Within a generation that participation had largely ended, and the mechanism was
the one described above rather than any formal exclusion. A landholding class
whose land is consumed by litigation stops being a political class. The
Californio delegates who helped write California's first constitution watched
their families' holdings pass to the lawyers who had represented them.

The treaty promised protection of property and delivered access to courts. In a
contest between a written guarantee and a procedure, the procedure wins.

## Indigenous title

Neither sovereign recognised it, before or after.

Mexican law had extended citizenship in principle without recognising Indigenous
land title in practice. American law did not extend either. Eighteen treaties
negotiated with California tribes in 1851 and 1852, which would have reserved
substantial territory, were sent to the Senate and never ratified; they were
placed under an injunction of secrecy for half a century. The tribes had ceded
their claims in the belief that reservations would follow. They did not.

There is no procedural complexity to describe here and no litigation to trace.
The claims were simply not recognised.

## What the chapter proves

Conquest becomes capital through documentation, and the documentation is where
the outcome is decided.

The fighting in California lasted seven months and changed very little. The
paperwork lasted forty years and changed everything: who owned the coast, who
owned the interior, who could borrow against it, and who was left holding a
sketch map and a lawyer's bill.

The legal framework is now in place. The gold has been in the river for two
weeks. And the largest voluntary migration in the history of the hemisphere is
about to arrive in a territory where the land is already owned, the title is
already contested, and the courts are three thousand miles away.
